title: Block close: the prayer book
hookLine: psalms for every mood, and wisdom that knows life is short and good

cards: Fifty days ago this part of the Bible opened with a tree planted by the water. Since then: a psalm for the night sky and a psalm for the dark night. My God, my God, why.
A clean heart, asked for after a terrible failure. Help from the hills. Out of the depths.
By the rivers of Babylon. Then Job, a good man who lost everything, and his friends, wise for seven days, until they started talking. Then Proverbs, the Preacher, the Song and Lamentations.
So what was all of it?

teach.h: THE PRAYER BOOK OF TWO FAITHS.
teach.b: Start with the Psalms. For many centuries they've been the prayer book of Jews and of Christians: monks chant all hundred and fifty in a cycle, churches sing them on Sunday, people whisper them in hospital beds.
And the surprise is how much of it isn't polite. There's joy, in the King James words: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." There's trust: the Lord is my shepherd.
But there's also rage, confusion, how long, O Lord, and one psalm, the eighty-eighth, that ends in darkness with no answer at all.
A large share of the psalms are laments. This prayer book teaches you to bring the real feeling, not the tidy one.
The early church writer Athanasius wrote that in the rest of scripture we read about others, but in the Psalms we find our own words, as if they were written for us.
The wisdom books keep the same honesty. Job won't accept a cheap answer for suffering, and in the end God says Job spoke rightly and his explainers did not.
Proverbs puts wisdom in ordinary life: the tongue, the work, the ant. The Preacher says life is breath, so eat your bread with joy. The Song says love is as strong as death.
Lamentations finds mercies new every morning, even in the ruins. Put together, one idea these books share is that everything a human being feels can be brought before God.
The Gospels show Jesus praying a psalm on the cross. Read like this, the prayer book isn't there to make anyone sound holy; it's there to make them honest.

how: Christians pray the Psalms daily in many forms: monastic communities and the Liturgy of the Hours cycle through them, Orthodox services read the whole Psalter each week, Anglicans pray them through each month, and many Protestants read one a day.

o: a formal prayer of thanks after a harvest
a hymn sung only at royal funerals
an honest cry to God from grief or pain

games.q: what's inside the block — tap the pairs.
p: a prayer book for every mood
refused a cheap answer for suffering
all is breath; eat your bread with joy

s: the Psalms are all songs of praise
a large share are laments, and Psalm 88 ends in darkness with no answer.
in Job, God says Job spoke rightly and his explainers did not
Job 42:7: the friends with tidy answers are the ones rebuked.
the Psalms are prayed by both Jews and Christians
they have been the prayer book of both for many centuries.

games.q: you're furious, or grieving, and you want to pray, but your feelings don't sound holy. what do the Psalms do?
o: wait until you feel calm, then pray.
bring the real feeling, rage and grief included.
pray only praise and keep the rest to yourself.
games.why: the Bible's prayer book is full of how long, O Lord and why. the psalms teach prayer that is honest before it is polite.

practice: Let some of the psalms pass by in your mind, the tree by the water, the Lord is my shepherd, as the deer, be still, shamar, De profundis, curiously wrought, and notice which one your heart leans toward: not the one you think you should choose, the one that sounds like you.
Keep it as your psalm for the year, for good days and bad. If you pray, you can pray its first line now.

wordCard.voice: Lament. The honest cry that fills much of the Psalms, the prayer book for every mood, with wisdom books just as honest.

orig.note: Hebrew name of the book of Psalms: praises, though many of them are laments.

carryVoice: Your line: pray what you feel. Exactly as it is, good or hard. A whole block, closed.
